ICE FLOATS ON WATER DUE TO ITS LOWER DENSITY COMPARED TO LIQUID WATER. THIS UNUSUAL PROPERTY ARISES FROM THE MOLECULAR STRUCTURE OF WATER. WATER MOLECULES ARE POLAR, WITH HYDROGEN AND OXYGEN ATOMS HAVING PARTIAL POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE CHARGES, RESPECTIVELY. THESE POLAR MOLECULES FORM HYDROGEN BONDS WITH EACH OTHER. 

WHEN WATER FREEZES, THE MOLECULES ARRANGE INTO A HEXAGONAL CRYSTALLINE LATTICE. THIS STRUCTURE CREATES SPACES BETWEEN THE MOLECULES, MAKING ICE LESS DENSE THAN LIQUID WATER. IN LIQUID WATER, MOLECULES MOVE FREELY AND ARE CLOSER TOGETHER, RESULTING IN HIGHER DENSITY. THE HYDROGEN BONDS IN SOLID ICE HOLD THE MOLECULES APART, REDUCING THE DENSITY AND ALLOWING ICE TO FLOAT ON WATER.
